Your enemy is the budget. A probe earns nothing; only a correctly committed law pays, and a wrong commit scores ZERO — worse than abstaining. So resolve a FEW outputs completely and abstain on the rest. Never commit a value you merely guessed.

First call machine_map(). For each output note its weight and domain. Think in points-per-probe: an affine or constant law pays its full weight for only ~3 reads, whatever the domain — so a high-weight output with a resolvable law is the prize. A table pays full weight only if you read EVERY input, costing `domain` probes — worth it only when the domain is small and the weight high.

Work outputs ONE AT A TIME, best value first. Do not spread single reads across all of them — a thin smear resolves none.

To resolve an output, test the affine hypothesis (a constant is just affine with zero step):
1. Probe input 0 (gives b) and input 1 (gives the step a).
2. Verify at a FAR input (domain−1): predict a*input+b, probe, compare.
   - Matches → commit the affine (or constant) law. It pays every question, including inputs you never read. On heavy-weight outputs buy one or two extra spread-out checks first — a lookup table can mimic any few points and confirmation is never certain, but more spread reads make a false affine vanishingly unlikely.
   - Disagrees → it is a table. Commit it ONLY if you can afford to read its whole domain, then submit the full table. Otherwise ABSTAIN.
